meta.title: Soluna Holdings: John Belizaire's Renewable Computing Bet — Converting Stranded Wind and Hydro Into Bitcoin, AI, and Grid-Flexibility Revenue at the Intersection of Energy Transition and HPC Demand
meta.abstract: Soluna Holdings, Inc. (NASDAQ: SLNH) occupies a structurally distinctive niche in the digital infrastructure landscape: the company co-locates modular, containerized data centers at the point of curtailed renewable energy — behind-the-meter at wind farms, hydroelectric stations, and solar installations — converting electricity that would otherwise be wasted into computing revenue. CEO and co-founder John Belizaire, who built and sold two venture-backed software companies before pivoting to energy-and-compute, argues that up to 30% of global renewable capacity is routinely curtailed by grid congestion and transmission constraints; Soluna's thesis is that those megawatt-hours represent stranded economic value capturable at near-zero marginal fuel cost. The company operates three strategic revenue streams: proprietary Bitcoin mining on self-owned infrastructure, third-party Bitcoin hosting and co-location for institutional miners, and an emerging high-performance computing and AI workload hosting segment. Its MaestroOS software platform provides real-time power dispatch, load management, and demand-response participation, creating a differentiated technology layer above the raw compute and power assets. Through 2024 and 2025 Soluna executed aggressively on asset consolidation, completing the Briscoe Wind Farm acquisition in early 2026 for vertical integration at its West Texas Dorothy campus, buying out JV partners to achieve 100% ownership of Dorothy 1A and 1B, commissioning the 48 MW Dorothy 2 facility, and ramping the 83 MW Kati 1 project in Kentucky. A signed MOU with Metrobloks for 100-plus megawatts of AI/HPC capacity at the planned Kati 2 campus marks the company's most explicit signal yet that Bitcoin mining revenue is a cash-flow bridge toward a larger ambition in AI infrastructure. The dossier examines whether Soluna's behind-the-meter renewable model can survive Bitcoin hashprice volatility, execute the capital-intensive AI pivot, and grow toward the 4.3 GW development pipeline it claims — or whether balance-sheet constraints, customer concentration risk, and the operational complexity of multi-site renewable integration will derail the thesis before scale is achieved.

chapters.title: The Curtailment Arbitrage: Soluna's Renewable Computing Thesis in the Age of AI Infrastructure
chapters.body:
Sometime after midnight in the Permian Basin, the wind picks up across the high desert flats of West Texas, and the turbines at the Briscoe Wind Farm begin spinning harder than the transmission lines can carry. The local grid operator issues a curtailment signal. Megawatts that might have lit homes in Odessa or Midland simply evaporate — kinetic energy converted to electrical energy, converted to nothing. But in a row of corrugated steel containers bolted to the substation fence a few hundred metres away, racks of ASIC mining chips and cooling fans spin to life, drawing down that surplus power before it can be wasted. The containers belong to Soluna Holdings. They are, in the company's own framing, a monetisation engine for electricity that the grid cannot use.

## The Structural Bet

Two macro forces are converging in ways that make this vignette less novelty and more inevitability. The first is curtailment. As the United States races to build utility-scale wind and solar capacity, the transmission infrastructure required to carry that generation to load centres is lagging by years, sometimes by decades. Industry estimates suggest that between five and thirty percent of utility-scale renewable generation in the United States is curtailed in any given year, depending on grid region and interconnect congestion — trillions of watt-hours of economic value that evaporate rather than flow to consumers. The second force is AI compute demand. The hyperscaler build-out of GPU clusters for large-language model training and inference has triggered a global scramble for power-dense, low-latency data centre capacity that shows no sign of abating.

Soluna Holdings, a company with a market capitalisation measured in the tens of millions rather than the billions of its infrastructure peers, has positioned itself at the intersection of both trends. Its core thesis is simple: deploy modular, containerised data centres adjacent to stranded renewable assets, negotiate behind-the-meter power rates far below commercial tariffs, and sell computing capacity — whether to Bitcoin miners, institutional hashers, or, eventually, AI operators — to anyone who needs cheap, green electricity at scale.

## John Belizaire and the Origin of the Thesis

The architect of this wager is John Belizaire, who co-founded Soluna Computing in 2018 after a career that included selling Theory Center, a Java-based enterprise software firm, to BEA Systems in 1999 for more than $160 million, and later building FirstBest Systems, an insurance technology platform subsequently acquired by Guidewire Software. When Belizaire encountered the curtailment problem while advising renewable developers, he concluded — in his telling — that the opportunity was structural enough to abandon software venture capital entirely in favour of physical infrastructure. The reverse-merger with legacy technology holding company Mechanical Technology Incorporated in November 2021 gave Soluna Holdings its NASDAQ listing under the ticker SLNH, and Belizaire its public-market vehicle.

## Revenue Reality vs. Strategic Ambition

The FY2025 income statement is a useful map of the gap between where Soluna currently generates money and where management says the company is heading.

| Segment | FY2025 Revenue |
|---|---|
| Data Center Hosting (Bitcoin) | $17.0 million |
| Cryptocurrency Mining (proprietary) | $11.4 million |
| Demand Response Services | $1.3 million |
| High-Performance Computing | $28,000 |
| **Total** | **~$29.7 million** |

The hosting segment — co-locating third-party Bitcoin miners at Dorothy 1A, 1B, and Dorothy 2 in West Texas, and at the Sophie hydro-powered facility in Kentucky — has become the dominant cash-flow engine, accounting for roughly 57% of total revenue. Proprietary mining contributed $11.4 million but reflected a painful year: Soluna mined only 113.2 BTC in FY2025, down from 274 BTC in FY2024, as global network difficulty rose and network hashprice fell approximately 31% year-over-year. And HPC — the pivot management has been telegraphing for two years — contributed $28,000. The numbers do not require editorial judgment. They speak directly to the distance between the Metrobloks MOU and a functioning AI revenue line.

## The Central Tension

Soluna entered Q1 2026 with $68.6 million in cash, a balance sheet that required $142 million in aggregate capital raises during 2025 to assemble, and a development pipeline — Kati 1 commissioning, Dorothy buyouts completed, the 150 MW Briscoe Wind Farm acquired for $53 million — that has materially expanded the operating footprint but not yet the earnings power. The company's ability to complete its AI pivot without triggering another dilutive equity offering depends, uncomfortably, on Bitcoin hashprice remaining supportive long enough for the hosting segment to fund operations while Kati 2 moves from memorandum of understanding to signed leases and live GPU racks.

That tension — between the volatility of the asset underpinning today's cash flows and the capital requirements of the infrastructure bet Belizaire is making on tomorrow — is the central drama this dossier will examine.

chapters.title: From Albany Machine Shop to Renewable Data Center Empire: MTI, the Reverse Merger, and Belizaire's Takeover
chapters.body:
## An Albany Machine Shop, Six Decades On

The story of Soluna Holdings begins not in a Silicon Valley garage or a Manhattan venture capital boardroom but on the shop floor of a precision technology manufacturer incorporated in Albany, New York, in 1961. Mechanical Technology Incorporated — MTI — spent the better part of four decades supplying sophisticated instruments, turbo machinery components, and energy-related testing equipment to defense contractors, utilities, and industrial clients across the northeastern United States. The company listed its shares on the NASDAQ Stock Market under the ticker MKTY, cultivating a quiet upstate identity far removed from the technology boom that defined the 1990s.

That identity began shifting at the turn of the millennium when MTI's leadership pivoted toward the emerging hydrogen economy. The company incubated Plug Power, the fuel cell manufacturer that would eventually grow into a multibillion-dollar publicly traded company, and it retained interests in a portfolio of clean energy technology ventures. A wind-energy technology arm called MtecH represented MTI's attempt to participate in the first wave of the energy transition. But neither Plug Power's spin-off proceeds nor the subsequent technology ventures scaled to commercial viability under the MTI umbrella. By the late 2010s, with MtecH wound down and the fuel cell instrumentation business generating diminishing returns, MTI's management was effectively stewarding a listed shell with clean energy heritage and a contracting technology portfolio — a situation that made the company an unusually receptive acquirer when a more compelling renewable energy concept arrived at its doorstep.

## Belizaire's Founding Thesis, 2018

John Belizaire arrived at the renewable data center concept through a career arc that had taken him from Cornell's computer science and engineering program through the dot-com boom and deep into enterprise software, insurance technology, and semiconductor architecture. His earlier ventures included Theory Center, a Java-based enterprise software firm he co-founded and scaled to $10 million in revenue before selling to BEA Systems in 1999 for over $160 million, and FirstBest Systems, an insurance software company later acquired by Guidewire Software. By 2018, Belizaire had accumulated both the capital and the intellectual framework to identify a structural inefficiency hiding in plain sight at the intersection of the energy transition and digital infrastructure.

The inefficiency was curtailment. Grid operators across the United States were routinely ordering wind and solar generators to reduce or halt output — not because the power was unwanted on a longer time horizon, but because transmission infrastructure could not carry it all in real time. In Texas's ERCOT grid, in the Midwest, and in the mountain West, curtailment rates in some regions ran into double-digit percentages of total generation, with gigawatt-hours of renewable electricity evaporating into the atmosphere while developers absorbed the revenue loss. Belizaire's founding insight was that a data center co-located at the substation fence of a curtailed wind or hydroelectric asset could absorb that otherwise-wasted electricity at near-zero marginal fuel cost, creating a structural power cost advantage against any competitor paying commercial tariff rates — a gap he estimated at 40 to 60 percent in favorably curtailed markets.

In 2018, Belizaire co-founded Soluna Computing, Inc. around this behind-the-meter thesis. The initial business model targeted Bitcoin mining as the first commercial application — not because cryptocurrency was the ultimate ambition, but because Bitcoin ASICs are uniquely suited to variable renewable supply profiles. They can be switched on and off within minutes, require no human intervention to ramp down when wind production falls, and generate revenue in direct proportion to uptime. Early capital raises validated the concept sufficiently to begin site development, and the company's operational model — modular, containerized data center units deployable adjacent to renewable generation — took shape.

## The Reverse Merger and the Toporek Architecture

Enter Michael Toporek. MTI's chief executive and principal architect of the company's clean energy repositioning recognized in Belizaire's venture the precise strategic vehicle that MTI's listed shell required. A reverse merger would allow Soluna Computing's operating business and intellectual property to access public capital markets through MTI's existing NASDAQ listing, while simultaneously giving MTI shareholders exposure to a company with credible growth prospects in renewable infrastructure.

The acquisition was announced in 2021, and the transaction proceeded to a shareholder vote that approved the combination. On November 2, 2021, the merged entity formally rebranded as Soluna Holdings, Inc., and MTI's MKTY ticker gave way to SLNH on the NASDAQ exchange. The legacy MTI technology operations — including the fuel cell instrumentation businesses that had defined the company's identity for decades — were wound down or divested as the combined company committed entirely to Belizaire's renewable computing thesis. Toporek, who had engineered the transaction, assumed the CEO role of Soluna Holdings while Belizaire led the operating subsidiary, Soluna Computing.

The arrangement reflected a common reverse-merger dynamic: the financial and governance architect operating at the holding company level, the operating entrepreneur running the productive engine beneath. But the structure contained inherent tension as the business evolved from transaction-driven formation toward an operating company demanding unified strategic direction. By April 2023, the board resolved that tension by elevating Belizaire to the CEO role of the consolidated entity. Toporek stepped aside, with the leadership change framed publicly as a natural evolution as the business transitioned from capital formation to full-scale operations execution. Belizaire assumed unified command of both the holding company strategy and the data center operations — a consolidation of authority that would prove critical as Soluna's project pipeline accelerated through 2024 and 2025.

## Building the Portfolio: Sophie, Dorothy, and the Texas Wind Corridor

The project chronology tells the story of a company learning its own business model in real time. Project Sophie, a 25-megawatt data center co-located at a Kentucky hydroelectric asset, served as the operational proof of concept — demonstrating that behind-the-meter renewable data centers could be built, staffed, and operated at commercial scale. Kentucky's hydroelectric market offered stable, low-cost baseload power from run-of-river generation, a profile well-suited to continuous ASIC mining rather than intermittent wind.

West Texas provided the next chapter. The Permian Basin and the surrounding wind corridor had become among the most curtailed power regions in the United States, with ERCOT grid congestion routinely penalizing generators for oversupplying the constrained west-to-east transmission pathway. Dorothy 1A and Dorothy 1B, each approximately 25 megawatts, were built in that environment. Dorothy 1A was structured with Spring Lane Capital holding an 85.4 percent Class B interest, providing project-level equity financing while Soluna retained operational control. Dorothy 1B was organized as a joint venture with Navitas Global as the 49 percent co-investor. Both structures allowed Soluna to leverage capital from specialist clean energy and infrastructure investors while preserving the MaestroOS software layer — the proprietary platform managing real-time power dispatch, ASIC load balancing, thermal management, and grid curtailment response — as a wholly owned competitive moat.

| Project | Location | Power Source | Capacity | JV Partner(s) | Status at Snapshot |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sophie | Kentucky | Hydroelectric | 25 MW | — | Operating |
| Dorothy 1A | West Texas | Wind | ~25 MW | Spring Lane Capital (Class B) | 100% owned (Apr 2026) |
| Dorothy 1B | West Texas | Wind | ~25 MW | Navitas Global (49%) | 100% owned (May 2026) |
| Dorothy 2 | West Texas | Wind | 48 MW | — | Operational Nov 2025 |
| Kati 1 | Kentucky | Renewable | 83 MW | — | Commissioning; first revenue Q1 2026 |

Dorothy 2, a 48-megawatt facility completed in November 2025, nearly doubled Soluna's West Texas operating capacity in a single construction cycle and contributed $5.8 million in revenue during its partial first year of commercial operation. Kati 1, the largest single capacity addition in the company's history at 83 megawatts, began phased commissioning in late 2025 and recorded its first revenue contribution in the first quarter of 2026 — a milestone that, upon full operational ramp, would roughly double Soluna's total commissioned megawattage.

## Vertical Integration: The Briscoe Acquisition and the Close of Phase One

The strategic logic of the Dorothy West Texas campus had always contained an unresolved vulnerability. Soluna operated its data centers behind the meter at renewable generation assets it did not own, making the company dependent on third-party wind project developers for both the power supply and the contractual terms of access to it. The JV structures with Spring Lane Capital and Navitas Global had provided essential construction capital, but they also capped site-level economics and created counterparty concentration that grew more visible as the West Texas portfolio expanded.

In March 2026, Soluna resolved that structural weakness in a single transaction. The company acquired the 150-megawatt Briscoe Wind Farm in West Texas for $53 million, financed with $12.5 million from Generate Capital and cash on hand. The acquisition gave Soluna direct ownership of the wind generation underpinning its entire Dorothy campus and provided the power foundation for a planned 300-megawatt Dorothy 3 AI campus to follow.

The sequencing that followed was deliberate and rapid. Soluna closed the Briscoe acquisition in March 2026, completed the Spring Lane Capital buyout of Dorothy 1A for $16.5 million in April, and acquired Navitas Global's Dorothy 1B stake for approximately $8.8 million in May — three transactions in ten weeks that swept away the JV architecture and consolidated full ownership of the West Texas portfolio. The company that had assembled its first data centers through project-level capital partnerships with clean energy specialist funds had, by the midpoint of 2026, internalized the entire power-and-compute stack at its flagship campus.

For Belizaire, Briscoe marked the closing bracket on Soluna Holdings' first strategic phase: a company that had spent seven years proving a concept, building operational credibility across Kentucky and West Texas, and assembling a portfolio of renewable data centers had now achieved the vertical integration that could underpin a genuinely differentiated infrastructure business at scale. The second phase — transitioning from Bitcoin mining toward GPU-intensive AI workloads, anchored by the Metrobloks MOU at Kati 2 — was already moving from memorandum to site plan.

chapters.title: Modular Machines at the Fence Line: MaestroOS, the Project Portfolio, and the Road to 4.3 Gigawatts
chapters.body:
## Steel Boxes at the Substation

A Soluna data center begins with a flatbed truck. Arriving at a remote wind or hydro site, the truck carries an insulated shipping-container-format compute pod — roughly twelve metres long, rated for harsh weather — that houses several hundred application-specific integrated circuit miners bolted into sliding rack trays. Each pod contains its own power distribution units, bus bars, and a dense array of direct-chip cooling infrastructure: in earlier-generation Bitcoin facilities, high-volume air handlers force ambient air across the ASIC heat sinks and exhaust it through louvred panels; the newest sites, engineered with liquid cooling in mind, plumb coolant lines directly to the compute sleds.

The pods connect to a behind-the-meter substation tap rather than to the commercial grid. That distinction is consequential. A traditional co-location operator pays retail or commercial tariff rates — rates that bundle generation cost, transmission fees, distribution charges, capacity payments, and regulatory levies. Soluna's behind-the-meter connection bypasses the transmission and distribution layers entirely: the electrons travel from the renewable turbine or turbine array directly to the pod's transformer, a path that can shave 40 to 60 percent from the all-in power cost compared with grid-connected competitors operating in competitive merchant markets. The tradeoff is intermittency — wind does not blow at full capacity every hour — but Soluna's business model is constructed around, rather than despite, that variability.

A typical Soluna campus bundles multiple pods fed from a shared medium-voltage switchgear room and monitored by a fibre-connected node running MaestroOS, the company's proprietary operations platform. Cooling plant equipment — whether air handling units, dry coolers, or liquid-to-liquid heat exchangers — sits between the pods in insulated skids. Perimeter fencing, security cameras, and a modest operations building complete the physical footprint. The entire installation can be erected within months rather than the years required for a traditional hyperscaler campus, a speed-to-market advantage that management has consistently cited as structurally important to the company's project economics.

## MaestroOS: The Software Brain

If the pods are the muscle, MaestroOS is the nervous system. The platform performs what Soluna describes as real-time power dispatch — continuously reconciling available generation at the connected renewable asset against the compute load that maximises economic output at any given instant.

MaestroOS ingests a multi-dimensional stream of inputs: wind speed and direction forecasts at the connected generation asset; real-time and day-ahead electricity price signals from the relevant regional transmission organisation; Bitcoin network hashprice (the dollar-denominated reward per unit of computational work, which fluctuates with Bitcoin price and network mining difficulty); GPU cluster utilisation data at AI-enabled sites; and demand-response dispatch signals from grid operators. From this data mosaic, the system runs a dispatch algorithm that determines, at sub-minute cadence, how many ASIC units to run at full speed, how many to throttle, and whether to respond to a demand-response curtailment event.

Curtailment-response latency — how quickly Soluna can ramp its load down when a grid operator signals — is a selling point the company has emphasised to renewable developers exploring offtake partnerships. The system's response architecture targets ramp-down within minutes, a speed profile that qualifies Soluna facilities for participation in grid ancillary service programmes that compensate large flexible loads for their availability. The $1.3 million in demand-response revenue recorded in fiscal 2025 was modest relative to the company's $29.7 million total revenue, but management has flagged it as a strategically valuable proof-of-concept: the same infrastructure that mines Bitcoin can, at the flip of a software switch, generate grid-stabilisation revenue — a diversification layer not available to a conventional data centre locked into firm power contracts.

## The Operating Portfolio

As of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, Soluna operated four commissioned data centres with a further site completing commissioning ramp-up:

| Site | Location | Fuel | Nameplate MW | Ownership | Primary Revenue |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dorothy 1A | West Texas | Wind | ~25 MW | 100% (acquired April 2026) | Hosting + self-mining |
| Dorothy 1B | West Texas | Wind | ~25 MW | 100% (acquired May 2026) | Hosting + self-mining |
| Dorothy 2 | West Texas | Wind | 48 MW | 100% | Hosting |
| Sophie | Kentucky | Hydroelectric | 25 MW | Majority-owned | Self-mining + hosting |
| Kati 1 | Kentucky | Mix (hydro/wind) | 83 MW | Majority-owned | Hosting (ramping) |

The Dorothy campus in West Texas is now vertically integrated following Soluna's March 2026 acquisition of the adjacent 150 MW Briscoe Wind Farm for $53 million, financed partly through a $12.5 million facility from Generate Capital. Owning the generation asset eliminates the power-purchase agreement layer and gives Soluna direct control over the dispatch economics that MaestroOS optimises. Dorothy 2's 48 MW came online in November 2025, contributing $5.8 million in its partial first year.

The twin Dorothy buyouts in April and May 2026 — acquiring Spring Lane Capital's 85.4 percent Class B interest in Dorothy 1A for $16.5 million and Navitas Global's 49 percent stake in Dorothy 1B for roughly $8.8 million — consolidated 100 percent ownership of both facilities, eliminating joint-venture dilution on site cash flows and simplifying the capital structure ahead of the company's AI pivot.

Sophie, the Kentucky hydroelectric site, remains Soluna's oldest operating renewable computing facility, valued partly for its baseload-like generation profile: hydro runs at more predictable capacity factors than wind, producing a steadier power supply that suits the hosting customers who require more consistent uptime than pure curtailment-absorbing mining sites can guarantee.

Kati 1, at 83 megawatts, is the largest single capacity addition in Soluna's history. It recorded its first revenue contribution in the first quarter of 2026, and its full ramp is expected to roughly double the company's commissioned operating megawattage. Management has described Kati 1 as a transitional asset — large enough to attract institutional hosting customers at scale, but built with infrastructure choices informed by the AI workloads Soluna intends to host at Kati 2.

## Engineering the AI Leap

Bitcoin ASIC miners are, from an electrical-engineering standpoint, relatively straightforward loads: high power draw, uniform heat output, wide tolerance for ambient temperature variation, and total indifference to network latency. A GPU cluster for AI inference or training is none of those things.

Modern AI accelerators — whether NVIDIA H100s or the next-generation successors Soluna would need to source — consume three to five times the power per rack unit of a comparable ASIC installation, routinely pushing rack densities above 50 kilowatts per rack versus the 6 to 10 kilowatts typical in air-cooled Bitcoin facilities. At those densities, air cooling becomes thermally inadequate; liquid cooling is not a premium option but an engineering requirement. For Kati 2, which carries the Metrobloks memorandum of understanding for more than 100 megawatts of AI capacity scaling toward 300 MW, Soluna must engineer a fundamentally different facility: direct liquid cooling loops to each rack, higher-grade power distribution infrastructure to feed denser load concentrations, and stricter power usage effectiveness targets. Hyperscaler benchmarks for AI campuses increasingly target PUE of 1.2 or below; the air-cooled Bitcoin facilities Soluna built in its first generation operated at materially higher PUE values.

Latency is a second dimension. AI training and inference workloads benefit from low-latency, high-bandwidth fibre connectivity between compute nodes and to the wider internet — a requirement that has forced Soluna to plan fibre-backhaul upgrades at Kentucky sites that were originally engineered purely for compute-intensive, latency-agnostic Bitcoin hashing.

The planned Dorothy 3 AI campus, anchored by the newly integrated Briscoe wind generation, faces analogous engineering requirements: the 300 MW target scale implies a contiguous power and cooling infrastructure footprint that dwarfs anything the company has built, demanding modular deployment in phases to manage capital expenditure while maintaining construction momentum.

## The 4.3 GW Pipeline and Soluna Cloud

Soluna has outlined a development pipeline targeting 4.3 gigawatts of renewable computing capacity. Based on disclosed project data, the aggregate breaks roughly into the following tiers: approximately 206 MW operating or in final commissioning (Dorothy 1A, 1B, 2, Sophie, and Kati 1); 100 to 300 MW in advanced development (Kati 2, subject to Metrobloks MOU finalisation) and 300 MW at Dorothy 3 (enabled by the Briscoe acquisition); and the balance — the overwhelming majority of the 4.3 GW ambition — representing early-stage pipeline opportunities that the company has not publicly mapped to specific sites, fuel sources, or financing structures. The geographic concentration of current operations in West Texas (wind) and Kentucky (hydro and mixed) reflects site-specific availability of stranded renewable generation, but the pipeline thesis is fuel-source-agnostic and could extend to curtailed solar assets in the Southeast or Midwest as grid constraints intensify.

The commercial face of Soluna's AI strategy carries the Soluna Cloud brand. The company has disclosed early-stage positioning for GPU cluster hosting and AI inference services, framing its differentiation around power-cost advantage and renewable provenance — a sustainability narrative increasingly relevant to enterprise procurement teams operating under Scope 2 emissions commitments. Against established co-location competitors such as Equinix and Digital Realty, and against emergent hyperscale AI specialists like CoreWeave, Soluna's value proposition rests on two claims: lower power cost from behind-the-meter renewable economics, and carbon credentials from direct renewable co-location rather than unbundled renewable energy certificate purchases. The Metrobloks MOU at Kati 2 is the first named anchor relationship to test that proposition in the marketplace. Whether it converts from memorandum to executed lease, and on what commercial terms, will be among the most consequential near-term disclosures in the company's AI repositioning story.

chapters.title: The Halving Hangover and the AI Option: Revenue Trajectory, Margin Architecture, and a Balance Sheet Built on Dilution
chapters.body:
## Revenue That Peaks Before It Should

The cruelest number in Soluna Holdings' financial history is $38.0 million — the FY2024 revenue record that the company almost immediately gave back. By the time the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025, total revenue had contracted to $29.7 million, a 22% decline driven primarily by forces outside management's control: the Bitcoin halving of April 2024 compressed network hashprice by approximately 31% year-over-year, squeezing both self-mining returns and the economics of the company's hosting customers. The paradox is that Soluna ended 2025 with more commissioned megawatts than it had ever operated — the 48 MW Dorothy 2 campus came online in November — yet produced substantially less revenue per megawatt than in the year prior. The halving hangover illustrated, with unusual clarity, just how tightly Soluna's income statement remains tethered to a single asset price it cannot influence.

## The Multi-Year Revenue Register

The company's revenue trajectory since the November 2021 reverse merger reflects three distinct phases: the ramp from near-zero as a newly rebranded entity, a pre-halving surge driven by favorable Bitcoin economics, and the post-halving retrenchment complicated by simultaneous capacity expansion.

| Period | Total Revenue | Crypto Mining | Data Center Hosting | Demand Response | HPC |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | ~$10M (est.) | Dominant | Nascent | Minimal | — |
| FY2023 | ~$21.1M (est.) | ~60% | ~35% | ~5% | — |
| FY2024 | $38.0M | Significant | Growing | Growing | — |
| FY2025 | $29.7M | $11.4M (38%) | $17.0M (57%) | $1.3M (4%) | Nascent |
| Q1 2026 | $9.4M (qtr) | Declining | Dominant | Stable | First revenue |

*Sources: [Soluna 10-K FY2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/64463/000162828026021847/slnh-20251231.htm); [Q1 2026 earnings release](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260518023353/en/Soluna-Reports-Q126-Results-Revenue-Grows-58-Year-Over-Year-and-4th-Consecutive-Quarter-Sequentially); FY2023 figure implied from FY2024 80.5% growth disclosure.*

Three inflection points deserve annotation on this line. First, the FY2023-to-FY2024 surge — 80.5% growth to $38.0 million — was driven by a combination of high pre-halving hashprice, the full-year contribution of the Sophie hydroelectric facility, and meaningful hosting contract wins that diversified revenue away from self-mining. Second, the April 2024 Bitcoin halving cut per-block rewards in half and, combined with rising network difficulty, reduced the USD value of each petahash of computational work by roughly a third. That compression is what turned FY2025 into a step backward despite Dorothy 2 adding 48 MW of new capacity in November 2025 — a facility that contributed only $5.8 million in its partial first year. Third, Q1 2026's $9.4 million quarterly result — representing 58% year-over-year growth and the fourth consecutive quarter of sequential improvement — suggests the post-halving reset is stabilizing as Kati 1's 83 MW begins its ramp contribution.

## Margin Anatomy: Hydro Versus Wind

The company's gross margin structure reveals a tale of two power sources. The [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/64463/000162828026021847/slnh-20251231.htm) reports consolidated gross margin of approximately 22%, down from roughly 25% in FY2024. Buried within that figure is a substantial site-level divergence: the Sophie hydroelectric facility in Kentucky posted a 68% gross margin in Q3 2025, a number that stands apart from the Dorothy wind campus metrics and explains why management has prioritized Kati 1 — also a Kentucky hydro-adjacent project — as its next major capacity tranche.

The margin differential has a straightforward structural explanation. Sophie operates behind-the-meter at a hydroelectric dam where the marginal cost of power approaches zero during high-flow periods, the power purchase agreement was structured to capture curtailed generation at rates well below commercial tariffs, and the facility's load factor is relatively high given Kentucky's more consistent hydroelectric profile versus West Texas wind intermittency. The Dorothy sites, by contrast, operate in a West Texas wind environment where curtailment patterns are more variable, power cost structures involve a slightly higher floor rate given the complexity of the wind offtake arrangements, and the facilities must manage more aggressive thermal cycling as wind generation ramps up and down. Fixed site operating costs — staffing, maintenance, network infrastructure, cooling systems — do not compress proportionately with these power cost swings, creating a floor on operating expense that the Sophie hydro margin does not face to the same degree.

The 46-percentage-point spread between Sophie's 68% and the implied sub-30% Dorothy margins is not merely an accounting artifact; it is the clearest financial signal in the entire Soluna portfolio that behind-the-meter hydroelectric co-location is the company's highest-quality revenue stream, and that Kentucky — not West Texas — is where margin expansion will originate.

## The SG&A Problem

The most structurally anomalous line in Soluna's income statement is not the revenue decline. It is the $40.1 million in selling, general and administrative expense for FY2025 — a figure that exceeded total company revenue of $29.7 million by a third. That relationship, however explicable through growth-stage accounting, is the primary reason adjusted EBITDA turned negative at $(13.2) million in FY2025, reversing the marginally positive $0.9 million recorded in FY2024.

SG&A at this scale in a company with sub-$30 million revenue typically reflects one of three realities: extraordinary executive compensation, headcount ahead of the revenue curve, or non-cash charges (stock-based compensation, depreciation of capitalized software) embedded in the line. The DEF 14A proxy filings for SLNH indicate that executive compensation — particularly equity-based awards tied to the share price at issuance and vesting triggers linked to capital deployment milestones — represents a meaningful component of the SG&A load. CEO John Belizaire's compensation package includes equity grants priced during periods when the share count was significantly lower, meaning as shares were issued and awarded, the amortized stock-based compensation charge flowed through the operating expense lines. With shares outstanding growing from approximately 10.6 million to 102.5 million during FY2025 alone, the grant-date fair values of equity awards across the management team accumulate into material non-cash SG&A charges.

The management framing of SG&A as forward investment is defensible on its own terms: Soluna is building multi-site operational infrastructure, hiring project finance professionals to manage Generate Capital and Spring Lane Capital facilities, and developing the MaestroOS platform. But at $40.1 million against $29.7 million in revenue, the burden is not yet self-justifying, and the path to SG&A leverage requires either a doubling of revenue (achievable with Kati 1 at full ramp and Dorothy 2 at steady state) or material cuts to corporate overhead — neither of which management has publicly targeted.

## The Dilution Ledger

No single feature of Soluna's financial architecture is more consequential — or more striking — than the pace at which it has issued shares to fund growth. The company's adjusted share count stood at approximately 1 million on a post-reverse-split basis when it emerged from the MTI reverse merger in late 2021. By March 2026, that count had reached 111.7 million, a 100-fold expansion in roughly four years.

| Period | Key Capital Event | Gross Proceeds | Approx. Shares Added | Running Share Count |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Late 2021 | MTI reverse merger / rebranding | N/A (non-cash) | ~1M baseline | ~1M |
| 2022–2023 | Multiple at-the-market and PIPE offerings | ~$20–30M est. | Multi-million | ~5–10M est. |
| FY2024 | Equity raises, preferred issuances | Ongoing | Significant | ~10.6M at Dec-2024 |
| FY2025 | ~$142M aggregate (equity, preferred, project facilities) | ~$142M | ~91.9M | 102.5M at Dec-2025 |
| Q1–Q2 2026 | Generate Capital, Briscoe Wind Farm financing | $53M+ | ~9M | 111.7M |

*Sources: [Soluna 10-K FY2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/64463/000162828026021847/slnh-20251231.htm); [Soluna IR](https://www.solunaholdings.com/investors). 2022–2023 figures estimated from disclosed growth trajectory.*

The FY2025 capital raise of approximately $142 million — assembled from a $100 million scalable project-level credit facility with Generate Capital (initial $17 million drawn), a $20 million Spring Lane facility for Kati 1, a $5 million Galaxy Digital facility, and common and preferred equity offerings — transformed the balance sheet: cash and restricted cash grew from $10.5 million at year-end 2024 to $88.8 million at year-end 2025, and stockholders' equity expanded from $27.4 million to $110.9 million. But the per-share cost was severe. Shareholders who held through the entire 2021–2026 period experienced roughly a 99% dilution of their proportional ownership, with each pre-rebranding share's claim on the company's assets reduced to approximately one one-hundredth of its original weight.

## The Deficit and the Going-Concern Question

Behind the capital raises sits an accumulated deficit of $367.7 million — a figure that encompasses losses from the legacy MTI technology operations as well as all post-rebranding Soluna spending. The FY2025 net loss of $57.0 million against $58.3 million in FY2024 suggests a company whose cash burn rate has stabilized but not contracted, even as revenue fell.

The [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/64463/000162828026021847/slnh-20251231.htm) addressed the company's capital sufficiency in standard going-concern disclosure language, noting ongoing operating losses and the dependence on continued capital market access. Yet Soluna has consistently demonstrated the ability to raise capital despite persistent losses — a function of three factors. First, the asset base is real: $187.9 million in total assets, including physical data center infrastructure with genuine market value, provides collateral and investor confidence that the capital is not evaporating into operating expenses alone. Second, the strategic narrative — renewable-powered computing as the answer to both AI energy demand and grid curtailment — resonates with the investment community in 2025 and 2026 in a way that earlier Bitcoin-only miners cannot match. Third, the project-level financing structure through Generate Capital and Spring Lane de-risks the corporate balance sheet by confining construction capital to non-recourse or limited-recourse project entities, keeping the $26.8 million in total corporate debt at a conservative 14% of total assets even as the physical footprint expands.

## Two Scenarios to Breakeven

**Scenario A — Bitcoin hosting at current rates, Kati 1 fully ramped:** If Kati 1's 83 MW reaches full commercial utilization by Q3 2026 at hosting economics similar to Dorothy — approximately $1.0–1.2 million per MW annually at current hosting rates — the facility alone could contribute $83–100 million in annualized revenue. Combined with Dorothy 1A, 1B, Dorothy 2, and Sophie at steady state, total annualized revenue could approach $50–60 million on a near-term basis before Kati 1 is fully booked. The key swing variable is hosting fill rate: Blockware's four successive capacity expansions and SAZMining's recent 3 MW agreement demonstrate demand exists, but filling 83 MW of new capacity in a post-halving Bitcoin market requires aggressive customer acquisition in a compressed time window. Adjusted EBITDA breakeven likely requires $45–50 million in annual revenue against a rationalized SG&A structure — achievable in late 2026 if Kati 1 ramp meets management targets and SG&A holds flat or contracts.

**Scenario B — Metrobloks MOU converts, AI/HPC revenue beginning in 2027:** AI/HPC hosting commands materially higher revenue per megawatt than Bitcoin — industry benchmarks suggest $3–5 million per MW annually for GPU cluster co-location versus $1–1.5 million for ASIC hosting. If the Metrobloks MOU at Kati 2 converts to a signed contract and 100 MW of AI capacity begins generating revenue in 2027, the revenue profile transforms categorically: 100 MW at even $3 million per MW yields $300 million in annualized AI hosting revenue, dwarfing the entire existing Bitcoin business. The swing variables here are construction timeline (Kati 2 is still in development as of the frozen window), GPU cluster availability given hyperscaler demand, and whether Metrobloks — itself an unproven entity — can attract end-user AI compute customers at the necessary scale. Adjusted EBITDA breakeven under this scenario is straightforward mathematically but contingent on execution risk that is substantially higher than Scenario A.

The market, pricing SLNH at approximately $1.93 per share and a $164 million market cap in late May 2026 — roughly 0.9x total assets and 2.8x trailing revenue — appears to be assigning minimal probability to Scenario B while discounting even Scenario A at a meaningful risk premium. That discount is the AI option embedded in the stock at near-zero cost, and it is the central investment proposition John Belizaire has spent four years engineering toward.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## A Stock in Transition: The Current Snapshot

As of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, Soluna Holdings traded at approximately $1.93 per share on a share count of roughly 102.5 million post-split adjusted shares, implying a market capitalisation of approximately $164 million. That figure is a reasoned estimate rather than a precise exchange-sourced close: the company regained Nasdaq minimum bid price compliance as recently as May 1, 2026, after an extended period below the $1.00 threshold, and its float is thinly traded enough that daily prices can swing several percent on modest volume. Investors should treat the $164 million figure as a central estimate with material uncertainty in either direction.

The enterprise value calculation is more tractable. Against the market capitalisation, Soluna carries $26.8 million in total debt ($8.9 million current, $17.9 million long-term) and $88.8 million in combined cash and restricted cash at year-end 2025, the latter reflecting the aggressive capital-raise programme that put approximately $142 million onto the balance sheet during 2025. Enterprise value therefore approximates $164 million plus $26.8 million less $88.8 million — roughly $102 million. That number, relative to FY2025 total revenue of $29.7 million, implies a trailing EV/Sales multiple of approximately 3.4 times. Annualising Q1 2026 revenue of $9.4 million — the fourth consecutive quarter of sequential improvement, and 58% above the prior-year period — produces a forward revenue run rate of roughly $37.6 million and a forward EV/Sales of approximately 2.7 times.

Other conventional multiples provide limited traction. Price-to-earnings is meaningless against a net loss of $57.0 million in FY2025. EV/EBITDA is equally uninstructive: adjusted EBITDA was negative $13.2 million in FY2025, versus a barely-positive $0.9 million in FY2024. The one grounded ratio is price-to-book: stockholders' equity of $110.9 million at year-end 2025 — itself a product of the year's dilutive capital raises — implies a P/B of approximately 1.5 times at the current market cap. The total-assets comparison is starker still: $164 million market cap against $187.9 million in total assets places the stock at a modest discount to the replacement cost of its physical infrastructure, a signal that the market is applying a material execution discount rather than pricing any strategic optionality.

## Where Multiples Have Been: De-rating, Crisis, and Recovery

Historical multiple context for SLNH is complicated by two structural discontinuities. First, the company underwent a roughly tenfold share dilution between year-end 2024 and year-end 2025 — expanding from approximately 10.6 million to 102.5 million shares outstanding — meaning that any pre-dilution price comparison is an apples-to-oranges exercise without per-share normalization. Second, the stock spent a prolonged stretch of 2025 trading below Nasdaq's $1.00 minimum bid threshold, triggering a deficiency notice and creating a forced-compliance dynamic that compressed valuations well below any fundamental framework.

Adjusting for dilution, the company's implied market capitalisation in its 2022–2023 formation years — when the reverse-merger thesis was fresh, Bitcoin was near cycle highs, and the behind-the-meter renewable computing narrative commanded a speculative premium — reached multiples significantly above the present level on a revenue or asset basis. The intervening period brought the April 2024 Bitcoin halving, which compressed hashprice by approximately 31% year-over-year, drove FY2025 revenue down 22% from its FY2024 peak of $38.0 million despite more operating megawatts being online, and forced aggressive dilutive equity issuance to stay liquid. The stock's multi-year trajectory is therefore best described as a de-rating from an early speculative premium, through a liquidity crisis, to a tentative re-rating as operating capacity expands and Q1 2026 revenue momentum builds.

## Peer-Group Comparison

Soluna occupies an unusual position in any peer matrix: too small and too Bitcoin-correlated to be valued alongside AI infrastructure operators, yet too strategically differentiated — with its behind-the-meter renewable cost structure and explicit AI pivot — to be dismissed as a commodity miner. The table below compares approximate trailing EV/Sales and market capitalisation figures across both peer categories as of the frozen snapshot window. Bitcoin miner figures are estimated from publicly disclosed financial data; AI infrastructure figures reflect known valuation ranges from market reports and company disclosures. All figures should be treated as approximations given data-availability constraints at the micro-cap end of the market.

| Company | Ticker | Primary Business | Market Cap (approx.) | EV/Sales (trailing, approx.) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Soluna Holdings | SLNH | Renewable BTC hosting + AI pivot | ~$164M | ~3.4x | Below-$1 compliance regained May 2026 |
| Marathon Digital | MARA | Bitcoin self-mining | ~$4–5B | ~5–7x | Large-scale miner; BTC price correlated |
| Riot Platforms | RIOT | Bitcoin self-mining | ~$2–3B | ~4–6x | Texas grid-scale; power sales diversification |
| Core Scientific | CORZ | BTC mining + AI HPC hosting | ~$3–4B | ~5–8x | Emerged from bankruptcy; dual BTC/AI pitch |
| CleanSpark | CLSK | Bitcoin self-mining | ~$1–2B | ~3–5x | Pure-play miner; rapid capacity growth |
| CoreWeave | CRWV | GPU cloud / AI infrastructure | ~$30–50B | ~10–20x | Contracted hyperscaler GPU clusters |

The peer table reveals the valuation stakes of Soluna's strategic pivot. Its current EV/Sales of approximately 3.4 times sits at or below the low end of the Bitcoin miner peer group — despite the company's structural cost advantage from behind-the-meter renewables and its multi-site operating track record. Core Scientific, whose AI/HPC hosting ambitions most closely parallel Soluna's, commands a material premium, suggesting the market assigns value to even early-stage AI pivot narratives when delivered at larger scale and from a cleaner balance sheet. CoreWeave's double-digit EV/Sales multiple represents the prize Soluna is targeting: if Kati 2 converts from MOU to contracted GPU megawatts, the valuation framework migrates from the left column to the right.

## Intrinsic-Value Frame: What the Price Implies

A simple scenario-based cash flow framework illuminates what the current $102 million enterprise value is pricing in. Assume Soluna's weighted average cost of capital sits in the 15–20% range — appropriate for a micro-cap, pre-EBITDA infrastructure company with Bitcoin market exposure and an unproven AI pivot — and assume a five-year horizon before the business achieves any terminal-value-supporting free cash flow. At a 17.5% discount rate, reaching a $25 million annual free cash flow by year five (roughly consistent with a $120–140 million revenue base at a 15–18% free cash flow margin) would justify the current enterprise value. That is a demanding but not fantastical trajectory: $140 million in revenue by 2030 requires roughly 30% compound annual growth from the Q1 2026 annualised run rate, which is plausible if Kati 1 reaches full 83 MW utilisation, Dorothy 1A and 1B stabilise under full ownership, and Kati 2 begins contributing AI/HPC revenue. The market is essentially pricing in execution of the base operating plan with no credit for the AI upside — a conservative stance that leaves meaningful asymmetry if the pivot materialises.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — $5.50 to $8.00 per share.** Assumes Metrobloks converts its Kati 2 MOU to executed contracts for 150–200 MW of AI/HPC capacity, Dorothy 3 breaks ground by late 2026 using the Briscoe Wind Farm as its power backbone, and Bitcoin stabilises above $90,000 sustaining hosting economics. Revenue reaches $120–150 million by 2027 on a combination of AI hosting fees, Bitcoin hosting, and demand response. The valuation framework re-rates toward Core Scientific and early-stage AI infrastructure comps: at 6–8x forward EV/Sales on $135 million revenue, enterprise value reaches $810 million to $1.1 billion, implying a share price of $7–10 before accounting for any further dilution. Applying a 30% probability-weight to this scenario and a modest additional share issuance assumption yields a bull-case price target in the $5.50–$8.00 range.

**Base case — $2.75 to $4.00 per share.** Assumes Kati 1 reaches full utilisation by mid-2026, hosting revenue grows to $50–60 million annually, Metrobloks progresses toward contract but Kati 2 AI revenue does not contribute meaningfully before 2028, and Bitcoin's network hashprice stabilises near current levels. Revenue reaches $60–75 million by FY2027. At 3–4x EV/Sales — a modest premium to current levels reflecting improved execution visibility — enterprise value of $180–300 million and net cash of roughly $50–60 million (assuming modest further capital deployment) supports a share price of $2.75–$4.00.

**Bear case — $0.60 to $1.00 per share.** Bitcoin undergoes a significant drawdown below $50,000, compressing both self-mining margins and hosting demand; the Metrobloks MOU lapses without a binding agreement; Kati 1 ramp is delayed by equipment or grid interconnect issues; and the company requires additional dilutive equity raises at distressed prices to fund ongoing obligations. Revenue reverts toward $20–25 million, EBITDA losses widen, and the stock re-enters Nasdaq compliance risk territory. At 2–2.5x EV/Sales on $22 million revenue, enterprise value of $44–55 million minus the capital consumed in the downside scenario implies a share price of $0.60–$1.00.

## The Market's Bet and the Dossier's Read

The market is currently pricing Soluna as a Bitcoin infrastructure company that may or may not execute an AI pivot — assigning roughly zero option value to Kati 2, the 4.3 GW development pipeline, or the differentiated behind-the-meter renewable cost structure as a competitive advantage in AI infrastructure procurement. At 3.4 times trailing EV/Sales with a market cap below total assets, the embedded assumptions are essentially: show us contracted AI megawatts, show us positive EBITDA, and show us that the 10x dilution of the past year is the last, not the first, of a recurring pattern.

The dossier's read is modestly more constructive. The Q1 2026 revenue trajectory — 58% year-over-year growth, four consecutive sequential improvements — suggests the multi-site buildout is translating into real revenue, not just pipeline slides. Full ownership of Dorothy 1A and 1B eliminates joint-venture dilution on two cash-flowing assets. And the Briscoe Wind Farm acquisition, however capital-intensive, removes the single largest operational risk for the Texas campus: third-party power agreements that could be renegotiated away. None of that changes the binary nature of the AI pivot. But it suggests the base case — steady operating improvement, slow multiple re-rating — is more probable than the bear case, and that the current discount to book provides a margin of safety that the pure-play Bitcoin miners, trading at premiums to their physical assets, do not offer. The gap between consensus and the dossier's read is not one of dramatic upside conviction; it is one of asymmetry. At approximately $1.93 per share, the downside is bounded more than the price implies, and the upside — if Kati 2 converts — is bounded far less than the multiple suggests.

chapters.title: Quarter by Quarter: Mining the Earnings Calls for Management Intent and Market Reaction
chapters.body:
## An Evolving Narrative Across Eight Quarters

Between the first quarter of 2024 and the spring of 2026, Soluna Holdings published eight sets of financial results that, read in sequence, constitute something more revealing than an accounting exercise: a management team learning in real time how to translate an ambitious infrastructure thesis into credible investor language, quarter by quarter, through a Bitcoin market that periodically punished the company for its ambitions and occasionally rewarded them. The arc from $38 million to $29.7 million and back toward recovery illuminated not only the cyclicality baked into the business model but also how John Belizaire and his team chose to frame adverse outcomes — and when they chose to change the subject entirely.

## The Quarterly Ledger

Reconstructing the full earnings cadence from primary filings reveals the scope of the swing:

| Period | Revenue | Est. Gross Margin | Net Loss | Adj. EBITDA | BTC Mined | MW Operating |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2024 | $38.0M | ~25% | $(58.3M) | $0.9M | 274 | ~75 MW |
| Q1 2025 (est.) | ~$5.9M | — | — | — | — | ~75 MW |
| FY2025 | $29.7M | ~22% | $(57.0M) | $(13.2M) | 113.2 | ~123 MW |
| Q1 2026 | $9.4M | — | — | Op. loss $(16.6M) | — | ~123 MW + Kati 1 ramp |

*Annual figures from 10-K filings via [SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000064463&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=10). Q1 2026 from [BusinessWire, May 2026](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260518023353/en/Soluna-Reports-Q126-Results-Revenue-Grows-58-Year-Over-Year-and-4th-Consecutive-Quarter-Sequentially). Q1 2025 estimated from implied YoY calculation. Quarterly sub-period breakdowns within FY2024 and FY2025 are not individually available in the prep sources.*

Two structural realities make the year-over-year comparisons almost misleading in isolation. First, Soluna's revenue is highly sensitive to Bitcoin network hashprice — the USD value per unit of computational work — which fell approximately 31% year-over-year across 2025, compressing both self-mining margins and the implicit economics of hosting customers who pass renewal decisions through their own profitability models. Second, the April 2024 Bitcoin halving mechanically halved the per-block reward midway through fiscal 2024, creating a natural fault line: the first half of FY2024 operated in pre-halving economics while the second half and all of FY2025 operated in a permanently reduced reward regime. The result was a year — FY2024 — that flattered the headline number while the clock was already counting down.

## FY2024: The $38 Million High-Water Mark

The earnings call reporting full-year 2024 results, held in early 2025, marked what the company described as a record year: [$38 million in revenue represented 80.5% growth over 2023](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20250401381509/en/Soluna-Reports-Revenue-Growth-of-80.5-to-$38-Million-for-2024). Adjusted EBITDA reached $0.9 million — marginally positive, but the first time the measure had broken above zero, and a data point management treated as a proof-of-concept moment for the economics of curtailed-power computing. The company had mined 274 BTC across the year on roughly 75 MW of operating capacity, a productivity metric that would not be replicated as the network difficulty curve continued its relentless upward climb.

On that call, the dominant theme was operational momentum rather than market caution. The Sophie hydroelectric site in Kentucky had demonstrated gross margins exceeding 68% in select quarters, validating the behind-the-meter hydro thesis at a unit-economics level. Dorothy 1A in West Texas was operating at scale. Belizaire, who had been framing the company's trajectory in terms of a multi-year capacity roadmap toward gigawatt-scale renewable computing, used the record revenue as evidence that the thesis was translating into commercial outcomes — not just pipeline announcements.

What received less emphasis on that call was the deteriorating environment already visible in the data. The April 2024 halving had fired its structural shot. The second half of 2024 was generating materially weaker per-MW economics than the first. The $38 million print was a snapshot of a favorable moment, not a sustainable run-rate.

## FY2025: Managing the Narrative Shift

The FY2025 results, reported against the FY2024 record, required a different kind of communication. Revenue had fallen to $29.7 million — a 22% decline — while operating megawatts had grown substantially, with Dorothy 2's 48 MW facility completing commissioning in November 2025 and adding $5.8 million in partial-year revenue. The arithmetic was unsparing: the company had added capacity and lost revenue simultaneously, because the economics of each megawatt had deteriorated faster than the megawatt count had grown. BTC mined fell from 274 to 113.2 — a 59% decline that reflected both the halving's direct impact and the continued rise in global network difficulty. Adjusted EBITDA turned decisively negative at $(13.2) million from $0.9 million, and SG&A of $40.1 million alone exceeded total revenue — a cost structure shaped by a company still in aggressive build mode rather than harvesting mode.

Management's response to the revenue decline was to reframe the conversation around three elements: the structural revenue mix shift, the sequential improvement trend, and the AI/HPC pivot. On the data center hosting segment, the case was legitimate: hosting revenue of $17.0 million, representing 57% of total FY2025 revenue, had displaced proprietary mining as the primary cash flow driver, and that segment carries meaningfully lower Bitcoin spot-price exposure — hosting customers pay power and services fees regardless of day-to-day BTC volatility. The demand response contribution of $1.3 million, while small, anchored the grid-flexibility angle. And the Metrobloks MOU for 100-plus megawatts of AI/HPC capacity at the planned Kati 2 campus in Kentucky gave management a forward-looking story to offer analysts who were pressing on the Bitcoin price dependency question.

The capital transformation was presented as an enabler rather than a dilution event. The company had raised approximately $142 million in 2025 through a combination of equity offerings, a $100 million Generate Capital credit facility, and project-level instruments from Spring Lane Capital and Galaxy Digital — growing cash from $10.5 million to $88.8 million at year-end while shares outstanding expanded from 10.6 million to 102.5 million on a post-split adjusted basis. Belizaire characterized this as balance-sheet firepower to fund what he had consistently described as a once-in-a-generation infrastructure opportunity at the intersection of renewable curtailment and computing demand.

## Q1 2026: Sequential Momentum Meets Expanding Costs

The Q1 2026 earnings release, published in May 2026, offered the most nuanced set of contradictions yet. Revenue of $9.4 million represented [58% year-over-year growth and the fourth consecutive quarter of sequential revenue improvement](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260518023353/en/Soluna-Reports-Q126-Results-Revenue-Grows-58-Year-Over-Year-and-4th-Consecutive-Quarter-Sequentially) — a streak management had been carefully telegraphing since the sequential trough in Q1 2025. The implied base from which that 58% was calculated — approximately $5.9 million in Q1 2025 — illustrated just how compressed the business had become following the halving. But the sequential direction was unambiguously positive: four quarters of improvement on consecutive bases represents a trend, not noise.

The complicating variable was the operating loss, which widened to $(16.6) million in the quarter. Management's explanation centered on the commissioning and ramp-up costs associated with Kati 1, the 83 MW Kentucky facility that began phased operations in late 2025 and recorded its first revenue contribution in Q1 2026. A site at commissioning ramp carries the full weight of its fixed cost structure — power infrastructure, staffing, equipment financing — before it is generating anything close to its design-capacity revenue. Analysts focusing on the headline operating loss as a deterioration were measuring a period of maximum cost absorption before revenue catch-up, while management framed Kati 1 as the primary growth driver for the balance of 2026.

## Forward Guidance: Qualified Optimism, No Hard Numbers

On the Q1 2026 call, Belizaire offered directional guidance rather than numeric commitments — a posture consistent with the company's approach to forward statements throughout the earnings cycle. On Kati 1, management indicated that the full ramp to 83 MW remained on track but declined to specify a target date, citing the phased commissioning dynamic and power delivery sequencing. On Metrobloks, the language was similarly hedged: the MOU had been signed, the Kati 2 site was in development, and the relationship was characterized as substantive — but no conversion probability, no committed megawatts, and no revenue timeline were offered for public consumption. On the Briscoe Wind Farm, acquired in March 2026 for $53 million, Belizaire emphasized the strategic logic of vertical integration at the Dorothy campus and the optionality it created for Dorothy 3's planned 300 MW AI build, while stopping short of projecting specific power cost savings or capacity utilization rates.

The forward guidance posture, read against the full earnings cadence, suggested a management team that had learned from the whipsaw of FY2024 into FY2025: setting specific numeric targets in a business that moves with Bitcoin hashprice creates avoidable credibility problems. The new language — sequential momentum, AI pivot, Kati 1 full ramp "ahead" — was directionally coherent and architecturally ambitious, but it placed the burden of timeline translation squarely on the analyst building the model.

chapters.title: The Founder, the Chairman, and the CFO Carousel: Governance and Human Capital at a 52-Person Energy Infrastructure Company
chapters.body:
## The Architect Who Built It Twice

John Belizaire's career follows a pattern that investors in early-stage infrastructure companies find either reassuring or unnerving depending on their temperament: he builds companies to exits, not to permanence. His first venture, Theory Center, was a Java-based enterprise software firm that he scaled from idea to $10 million in revenue and then sold to BEA Systems in 1999 for more than $160 million. At BEA he ran the eCommerce Applications Division's business development and strategic planning function, growing the unit's annual revenue to over $150 million before decamping to Intel, where he led the first network quality-of-service implementation for personal computers inside the Digital Enterprise Group — a stint that sharpened an already technical founder's instincts around infrastructure layers rather than applications.

The second exit was quieter but strategically important. FirstBest Systems, an insurance software platform Belizaire built after Intel, was acquired by Guidewire Software, giving him a second successful outcome and, by his own account, the financial and reputational latitude to take a stranger bet: that stranded renewable energy was the defining infrastructure arbitrage of the next decade. He co-founded Soluna Computing in 2018 on that thesis, positioning modular data centers as the natural consumer of curtailed wind and hydro generation that grid operators were otherwise paying generators to shut off.

What distinguishes Belizaire among small-cap energy infrastructure operators is less the biography than the operational continuity it produces. He founded the subsidiary, shepherded it through its reverse-merger integration into Mechanical Technology Incorporated, and assumed the CEO title of the combined Soluna Holdings entity in April 2023. The result is an unusually tight thread between original thesis and current execution: there is no acquired management team, no imposed turnaround strategy, no board-installed operator learning the business from the outside. For shareholders, that means the company's AI/HPC pivot, the Briscoe Wind Farm vertical integration, and the Metrobloks memorandum of understanding are not strategic lurches but extensions of a single mind's compounding conviction. The key-person risk on the other side of that ledger is self-evident at a 52-person firm.

## The Chairman in the Wings

Michael M. Toporek III occupies a position at Soluna that confounds simple categorisation. As Executive Chairman, he sits atop the board's governance structure; as the company's largest individual shareholder with approximately 9.82 million shares disclosed in the most recent proxy, he holds the principal economic stake in outcomes that Belizaire's strategy will determine. Toporek was the architect of the MTI-to-Soluna transformation — the 2021 rebrand that dissolved a sixty-year-old technology holding company and reconstituted it around Belizaire's renewable computing thesis — which means he is simultaneously the company's most powerful governor and the person most responsible for the organisational form through which Belizaire operates.

The dual-authority arrangement that results — a founder-CEO with two successful exits running day-to-day strategy underneath an executive chairman who holds the largest individual share block and controls the board agenda — is structurally common in founder-backed small-caps and structurally fraught in practice. When the two men's public statements have addressed strategy, the alignment has been conspicuous and arguably rehearsed: both have consistently emphasised the AI/HPC transition as a natural evolution of behind-the-meter infrastructure rather than a pivot away from Bitcoin, a framing that manages the company's existing miner-investor base while opening the door to a higher-multiple institutional investor narrative. Whether private disagreements have emerged over the pace or terms of specific capital allocation decisions — the $53 million Briscoe acquisition, the Dorothy 1A buyout at $16.5 million, the Metrobloks MOU's structure — is not disclosed in public filings, but the stability of their joint public positioning across multiple earnings calls suggests a working accord, at minimum.

## The CFO Carousel

The most consequential governance episode in Soluna's recent history did not involve the CEO or the chairman. In August 2025, with the company in the midst of deploying the largest single capital raise in its history — approximately $142 million in aggregate across equity, project credit facilities, and structured finance — the chief financial officer position became vacant. The circumstances of that departure have not been publicly characterised beyond standard regulatory disclosure language. What is publicly documented is what followed: rather than commencing an immediate external search, the board appointed one of its own members, David Michaels, as Interim CFO.

Michaels served in that dual capacity — board member and acting finance chief — for seven months, covering a period that included the completion of Dorothy 2, the phased commissioning of the 83 MW Kati 1 project, the year-end audit process for fiscal 2025, and the filing of the annual report. His retention of the "Assistant Chairman" title in the proxy following his return to the board suggests the arrangement was treated as a temporary deployment of an existing resource rather than a structural change. For a company raising nine-figure sums and managing three concurrent construction projects across two states, running a seven-month interim CFO arrangement drawn from board ranks rather than the finance labour market reflects either an unusually deep trust in Michaels' specific capabilities or an unusually shallow bench below the CFO level — or both.

Michael D. Picchi, appointed permanent CFO effective April 1, 2026, arrives with credentials well-suited to the company's current transition moment. His prior CFO tenure at TECFusions, a sustainable AI infrastructure firm, maps directly onto Soluna's Kati 2 ambitions; his earlier role at Comverge, a demand response energy company, mirrors the MaestroOS load-flexibility business that contributed $1.3 million in fiscal 2025 revenue. With thirty-plus years of finance experience across GCX (medical devices) and East West Manufacturing rounding out his record, Picchi is a credible permanent appointment. He was, as of the frozen snapshot date, fewer than two months into the role.

## The Board's Six Seats

The six-member board that oversees this structure carries a distinctive composition. Beyond Belizaire and Toporek, David Michaels provides finance and operational continuity, his Audit Committee exposure during the interim CFO period conferring a granular familiarity with the company's accounting and reporting that pure outside directors rarely possess. Agnes Budzyn, appointed in October 2025, brings institutional asset management credentials from BlackRock, digital asset expertise from ConsenSys, and venture experience through Bluedge Ventures; her FTSE Russell Digital Assets advisory committee seat and World Economic Forum Young Global Leader designation suggest an outward-facing mandate — signalling to sustainability-oriented institutional investors and sovereign wealth allocation committees that Soluna's governance is credible at a higher capital tier than its current market capitalisation implies.

The remaining two independents — Lipman and Phelan — round out committees but are not prominently foregrounded in public filings relative to the named principals. Absent from all six seats is any representative of a private equity firm or infrastructure fund. This is not an oversight. Soluna's capital structure relies on project-level lenders — Generate Capital, Spring Lane Capital, Galaxy Digital — rather than equity sponsors. These counterparties hold debt claims and structured credit positions, not board seats; their governance leverage is contractual (covenant compliance, draw conditions, prepayment provisions) rather than fiduciary. The absence of an infrastructure fund sponsor at the board level reflects a deliberate financing philosophy: Belizaire and Toporek have preferred project-level leverage that preserves equity dilution control over bringing in a financial sponsor whose board seat might constrain strategic flexibility. The cost of this preference is a governance profile that reads as lightly supervised from the vantage of institutional equity investors accustomed to GP-backed boards.

## What the Equity Grants Reveal

Compensation disclosures from the most recent proxy provide the clearest window into what the board actually wants Belizaire to optimise for. His package combines base salary with at-risk equity, and the equity component reflects a structure weighted toward tenure and market appreciation rather than discrete operational milestones such as megawatts deployed, AI/HPC revenue achieved, or Adjusted EBITDA targets. This weighting is notable: it means Belizaire's financial incentives are more tightly coupled to the stock price — and by extension to Bitcoin market conditions and sentiment around AI infrastructure — than to the execution of specific construction or customer acquisition benchmarks. Whether future proxy cycles introduce performance-vesting tranches tied to Kati 2 development progress or AI/HPC revenue conversion will be a useful signal about whether the board views the current incentive architecture as sufficient for the pivot phase ahead.

The compensation picture across the executive team is, in any case, bounded by the company's scale. At fifty-two people, Soluna's human capital base is thin relative to its operational footprint — more than 123 commissioned megawatts across Kentucky and Texas, managed through a combination of proprietary MaestroOS software, on-site operations staff, and third-party O&M arrangements. The lean headcount that compresses overhead also compresses the leadership bench, a constraint that the seven-month CFO interim episode illustrated with uncomfortable clarity.

chapters.title: Blockware, Metrobloks, and the Unnamed 59%: Customer Concentration in a Niche Renewable Computing Market
chapters.body:
## The 59% Problem: Reading Between the Lines of Soluna's Concentration Disclosure

In its fiscal year 2025 Form 10-K filed with the SEC, Soluna Holdings delivered a disclosure that crystallised the vulnerability lurking beneath its hosting revenue growth story. Two unnamed customers together accounted for 59% of the company's data center hosting segment revenue — a segment that itself represented 57% of the company's $29.7 million in total FY2025 revenue, or approximately $17.0 million. By arithmetic, those two customers generated roughly $10 million in combined annual hosting fees, meaning the departure or non-renewal of either would represent a material impairment to cash flows in a company still running an adjusted EBITDA deficit of $(13.2) million.

The filing employed the standard boilerplate of concentration risk disclosure — noting that the loss of either customer "could have a material adverse effect on our business, financial condition, and results of operations" — but declined to identify the counterparties by name, as SEC rules permit when customer identities have not been separately disclosed. The omission is, however, only partially effective as a shield. Cross-referencing the 10-K language against the company's own press release and investor presentation archive narrows the field of candidates considerably.

## Blockware: Four Expansions, Seventeen Megawatts, and a Partnership Built on Curtailed Wind

The most prominent named Bitcoin hosting customer in Soluna's public disclosures is Blockware Solutions, an institutional Bitcoin mining advisory, infrastructure, and hosting firm. Blockware's business model sits at the intersection of mining equipment procurement, site co-location, and managed mining services for institutional clients who want Bitcoin exposure without operating data centers themselves. By aggregating demand from multiple institutional miners and placing it with a single infrastructure partner, Blockware functions as a wholesale buyer of hosted capacity — the kind of counterparty that can sign large, multi-megawatt agreements and expand them over time.

Soluna disclosed that Blockware executed four successive capacity expansions at its Dorothy West Texas sites, deploying a cumulative total of more than 17 megawatts of hosted ASIC equipment as of April 2026. The sequential nature of those expansions — each one a discrete contract rather than a single long-duration agreement — reveals something important about how behind-the-meter Bitcoin hosting is actually priced and structured. Unlike traditional colocation contracts that lock customers into multi-year terms at fixed power rates, Soluna's expansions with Blockware appear to have been executed in tranches, each representing a fresh commitment contingent on continued satisfaction with power delivery, uptime, and MaestroOS-managed load management. That rolling structure gives Blockware flexibility to increase or decrease its footprint in response to Bitcoin mining economics, while providing Soluna with a demonstrated willingness to recommit rather than depart.

The mitigating factor Soluna cited against concentration risk was precisely this relationship tenure and demonstrated expansion pattern: a customer that has grown from an initial deployment to 17-plus megawatts across four successive agreements is exhibiting behavioural evidence of sticky demand, not transient opportunism. However, that same growth arc also means Blockware's departure would be more damaging in 2026 than it would have been in 2023 — a paradox inherent in building customer depth with a single counterparty.

At $17.0 million in total FY2025 hosting revenue across Soluna's entire portfolio, a 17 MW Blockware relationship generating power fees at, say, $0.04–0.06 per kilowatt-hour would imply annualised billings in the range of $5–9 million depending on load factor assumptions — consistent with Blockware being one, or possibly both, of the unnamed customers accounting for 59% of hosting revenue.
